How One Creator & a Swarm of AI Agents Built a 5-Minute Cyberpunk Fashion Masterpiece in 19 Hours

Last week, @anabology dropped a public Google Drive with the master files for "ESCAPE VELOCITY"—a 5:06 lyric music video and cyberpunk fashion show that looks like a high-budget Studio Trigger x Balenciaga production:

In the film, an AI runway model walks the Silicon Valley zeitgeist as a split-flap terminal board counts down "18 MONTHS TO ESCAPE THE PERMANENT UNDERCLASS" until it flips to "THERE IS NO UNDERCLASS" and the catwalk lifts into orbit.

It was made in 19 wall-clock hours with ~50 human steering messages.

Inside the archive is a 6-page production post-mortem ("How ESCAPE VELOCITY was made"). It is the cleanest blueprint ever published on how autonomous agents, deterministic code, and generative models intersect.

Here is the exact technical breakdown of how it was built:

1. THE HUMAN-AI DIVISION OF LABOR: "Agents in parallel, one human with taste"

Most people treat AI like a slot machine: roll a prompt, get generic slop, complain about quality.

anabology flipped the architecture: the human supplies taste, curation, and decisive boundary conditions; Claude Code orchestrates the labor.

Claude ran over 40 specialized subagents across the pipeline:
• Research & Verification: A 31-agent workflow harvested SF tech culture, live memes, and longevity lore. Every claim was fact-checked by an independent verifier agent.
• The Writers’ Room: 4 lyricists competed across different axes (Density, Tension, Hook, and Fashion). Judge agents scored them, an aggregator merged the top lines, and a critic pass refined the meter.
• The Director Swarm: 3 director agents storyboarded the song independently (Fashion Film vs. Narrative vs. Meme Density). A head director merged them into 141 shots across 9 chapters.
• Chapter Animators: Dedicated animator agents wrote JavaScript animation code chapter by chapter, while an art-director agent reviewed rendered frames and requested fixes in a tight feedback loop.

Human input across the entire 19 hours? About 50 short messages.

2. THE UNIVERSAL CLOCK: Word-Level Forced Alignment

Before generating a single pixel of video, anabology established a strict mathematical timebase.

After Suno v6 generated the 5:06 electroclash track (which subtly accelerates from 131.5 to 133.9 BPM), the audio was processed locally on an RTX 3090 Ti:
• Stems separated via htdemucs
• Beat map extracted
• Word-level forced alignment generated via wav2vec2 (producing exact millisecond start and end timestamps for every single syllable)

Every camera cut, kinetic typography strobe, and scene transition across all 141 shots was locked directly to this timecode grid.

3. SOLVING CHARACTER CONSISTENCY WITHOUT REFERENCE IMAGES

Midjourney v8.2 lacks native --oref support. Maintaining a recognizable protagonist across 130 plates seemed impossible, so three methods were tested:
1. GPT-image identity passes: The aesthetic drifted away from Midjourney’s photographic texture.
2. Face-sheet image prompts (--iw 0.5): Caused severe over-conditioning (producing a close-up-sized head awkwardly pasted onto distant bodies).
3. The Solution: A Strict Written Canon + Demographic Anchor

The winning formula was defining her identity entirely in text:
"a young Caucasian American woman with pale skin and light freckles, black blunt jaw-length bob, one clay-orange streak, an eight-pointed clay spark hair clip, headset microphone, white cropped puff-sleeve shirt, black pleated coated-nylon skirt with harness belt and garment tag, knee boots."

By hardcoding this exact canonical description into every prompt alongside a consistent visual syntax ("blue-black and steel blue, one small red status lamp as the only warm light, fine silver grain, cinematic 35mm film still, no text, no letters, no logos"), Midjourney held character identity across all 130 plates without face swaps or LoRAs.

4. THE SEEDANCE DRIFT-DETECTION HACK

The most innovative engineering breakthrough in the project solved AI lip-sync drift.

When feeding an image plate and audio slice to Seedance 2.5, Seedance re-encodes the reference audio into its own soundtrack. When lip-sync fails, it is because Seedance's internal audio drifted from the input.

anabology realized this and wrote an automated validation script:
1. Seedance generated the shot.
2. The script compared Seedance's returned soundtrack against the master vocal using spectral cross-correlation.
3. The moment correlation dropped below a threshold, the script cut the shot on the last preceding eighth note.
4. A continuation clip was automatically launched starting from that exact frame to cover the rest of the bar.

86% of all sung seconds were mathematically verified in sync on the first pass (with LatentSync as a fallback). Total video gen cost: $93 for 91 submissions (421 seconds of 720p footage).

5. DETERMINISTIC CODE ON TOP OF THE PLATE: Frame = f(t)

Why do the typography and UI graphics look razor-sharp instead of morphing like normal AI video?

Because they were never generated by an AI video model.

The video models (Seedance / Midjourney) only provided the background "plate."

The meaning—kinetic typography, garment tags, split-flap countdowns, and object-tracking boxes (tracked via Grounding DINO)—was drawn by a custom JavaScript engine running in Headless Chromium (HTML5 Canvas + WebGL print pass).

Every single frame was a pure mathematical function of time:
Frame = f(t)

No guessing, no flickering, no hallucinated spelling errors.

6. POST-COLORIZATION: Rescuing Washed-Out Generations

When Seedance clips generated from monochrome frames returned desaturated and grey, anabology did not re-roll.

They used Exemplar-Based Video Colorization (Deep Exemplar, CVPR 2019), using the shot's original full-color Midjourney plate as the color exemplar.

The rule: Keep generation inputs in color, and apply artistic grading in post.

7. THE FULL PRODUCTION BALANCE SHEET

• Song: Suno v6 (1 full take, 5:06.4 at 131.5 -> 133.9 BPM)
• Plates: Midjourney v8.2 (188 prompts, 636 images, 130 plates used)
• Moving Video: Seedance 2.5 (91 submissions, 421s generated) -> $93
• Agents & Code: Claude Opus 5.5 (1.4B tokens, 96% prompt-cache reads) -> $626 API equivalent
• Final Render: Headless Chromium (7,354 frames, 1080p CRF 16 master) -> ~63 min local render
• Total Investment: 19 Hours Wall-Clock Time, ~$720 total compute

THE BIG LESSON: Taste is the Moat

Escape Velocity is proof that prompt engineering is dead. The new discipline is Creative Systems Engineering:
• Log and quantify your taste profile
• Run swarms of agents in parallel to draft, verify, criticize, and code
• Use AI for visual plates, but use deterministic code for meaning and typography
• Let the human spend 100% of their energy on high-leverage taste decisions

Full credit to @anabology for open-sourcing the blueprints. Study this pipeline. (some of this analysis might be correct, lol)

How to design rewards for post-training frontier image models? 

Our research suggests human preference reward is necessary, but insufficient: A preference model may still reward outputs that look appealing but miss details, introduce unrequested content, or exhibit other forms of reward-hacking.

We therefore optimize towards a composite reward:
- Bradley-Terry reward model trained on ~5.6M pairwise human votes
- Faithfulness reward from auto-generated prompt checklists evaluated by a vision-language model
- Constraint reward covering explicit and implicit user intent
- Anti-reward-hacking rubric rewards targeting failures such as garbled text and photorealism drift
This post-training recipe improves two already-strong open image models:
- Post-trained FLUX.2-dev gains 69 Elo points on our live T2I leaderboard, scoring 1202
- Post-trained Ideogram 4 gains 20 Elo points reaching a score of 1224 and surpassing all publicly listed open models (as of Sep 04, 2026).

Offline ablations with Gemini 3.5 Flash as the judge, show that these reward components are complementary: win rate against the base model increases as we add faithfulness and then constraint rewards on top of preference-only training, reaching 64.2%.

Finally, we ensemble policies trained with and without the anti-reward-hacking objective directly in weight space, further increasing win rate to 66.0%.

1. STOP TRYING TO DO EVERYTHING.

AI content creation is ridiculously broad.

And one of the biggest mistakes I see beginners make is trying to learn everything at once.

Today you’re creating AI ads.

Tomorrow you’re creating music videos.

The next day you’re doing AI influencers.

Then animation.

Then storytelling.

Then product photography.

Then motion graphics.

Then podcasts.

Before you know it, you’ve touched 15 things and mastered absolutely nothing.

Even something like AI advertising has sub-niches.
You could specialize in:

UGC ads, cinematic commercials, product ads, fashion ads, real estate ads, food ads, storytelling commercials, e-commerce ads…

The same applies to AI storytelling, AI music, image generation and almost every other category.

Pick something.

Become ridiculously good at it.

Give yourself at least 90 days of focused execution before deciding it isn’t working.

You don’t need to become known for everything.

You need people to associate your name with something.

[1/n] Introducing Diffusion Reward Models (DRM)

Reward Models are at the core of LLM post-training. But almost all of them make the same simplification:
they collapse human preference into a single score.

The problem is that human feedback is often not a point — different people can hold distinct, even conflicting, judgments about the same response.

So we asked: Can a Reward Model learn the distribution of human preference?

Here’s what we found 👇

📄 Paper: https://t.co/e0EMNa3I64
💻 Code: https://t.co/KVosB5D5PI
🤗 Models: https://t.co/wwdDpOtgbL

[2/n] Our answer is DRM: model rewards as distributions.

Instead of predicting a scalar, DRM replaces the conventional value head with a lightweight Diffusion Reward Head.

Given a prompt-response pair, it generates samples from the reward distribution.

So disagreement, uncertainty, and multiple plausible judgments can remain in the reward itself, rather than being averaged away.

And the same framework works with both multi-attribute rewards and pairwise preferences.
